title: 'Walking'
description: Published in the Atlantic Monthly in June 1862, a month after Thoreau's death: the great essay on walking, wilderness and the preservation of nature.
plot_or_argument: Thoreau argues that walking is a religious exercise, that the west and the wild are the true America, and that 'in wildness is the preservation of the world'; he calls for the protection of the forests and the creation of public parks.
historical_context: The 1850s, the settlement of the American west, the railroad, and the early conservation movement.
literary_significance: 'Walking' is the founding text of the American conservation movement and one of the most important essays on the natural world: its call to preserve the wilderness led to the national park system and to the modern environmental essay.

title: The Maine Woods
description: Published in 1864 after Thoreau's death: accounts of three journeys to the Maine woods in 1846, 1853 and 1857, and the finest American writing on the northern forest.
plot_or_argument: Thoreau describes the wilderness of Ktaadn, the moose hunt, the Indian guides, the logging camps of the Allegash and the East Branch, and the meeting of the industrial and the primitive at the edge of the forest.
historical_context: The 1846-57, the Maine lumber industry, the Penobscot and the native communities of the north, and the American debate on the preservation of the forests.
literary_significance: The Maine Woods is the greatest American book of the northern wilderness and one of the first to record the destruction of the North American forest: it is the founding text of the American literature of conservation and a central work of nineteenth-century writing on the Native American.

title: Woman in the Nineteenth Century
description: Published in 1845 and the first major American feminist book: an expanded version of the Dial essay 'The Great Lawsuit' and the foundation of the American women's movement.
plot_or_argument: Fuller argues that the soul has no sex, that the woman question is the question of whether every human being is allowed to grow according to her own nature, and that the separation of men's and women's spheres has mutilated both; she surveys the history of women and calls for their full participation in the life of the mind and of the state.
historical_context: The 1844, the Transcendentalist circle, the American woman question of the 1840s, and the European feminism of George Sand and the Utopian socialists.
literary_significance: Woman in the Nineteenth Century is the founding text of American feminism and the most important American book on women before The Second Sex: it established the demand for women's intellectual and political independence as a matter of principle, and it shaped the Seneca Falls Declaration of 1848.

title: Summer on the Lakes, in 1843
description: Published in 1844 and Fuller's first book: an account of a journey through the Great Lakes and the prairies, with portraits of the Indians, the settlers and the emigrant women.
plot_or_argument: Fuller travels from Niagara to Milwaukee and the prairie, and records the scenery, the societies of the frontier towns, the condition of the Native Americans, the lot of the emigrant women and the fate of the Indian woman Mariana.
historical_context: The 1843, the westward emigration of the 1840s, the forced removal of the Indians, and the Transcendentalist interest in the West.
literary_significance: Summer on the Lakes is the finest American travel book by a woman of the 1840s and a founding text of the literature of the American West: its account of the Native Americans and of the emigrant women makes it a key document of the American frontier.

title: Papers on Literature and Art
description: Published in 1846 and the first collection of literary criticism by an American: essays on British, French and American literature and on the art of the American landscape.
plot_or_argument: Fuller writes on Emerson, Hawthorne, Byron, Goethe, George Sand, the American poets and the question of whether there is an American literature; the volume includes the essays from the Dial and the Tribune.
historical_context: The 1846, the New York literary world, the American magazine culture of the 1840s, and the debate on national literature.
literary_significance: Papers on Literature and Art is the first substantial body of American literary criticism and a key text in the formation of the American canon; Fuller's estimate of Hawthorne and her advocacy of Goethe and Sand shaped the American reception of European literature.

title: These Sad but Glorious Days: Dispatches from Europe
description: Written for the New-York Tribune between 1846 and 1850 and collected posthumously: Fuller's dispatches from Italy during the revolutions of 1848-49 and the siege of Rome.
plot_or_argument: Fuller reports the Italian risorgimento, the election of Pius IX, the revolution in Rome, the defence of the Roman Republic under Mazzini and Garibaldi, and the French siege of 1849, in which she served as a hospital director.
historical_context: The 1846-50, the Italian revolutions, the Roman Republic, and the American reception of European radicalism.
literary_significance: Fuller's Roman dispatches are among the finest American war correspondence of the century and the first book of foreign correspondence by an American woman: they are a central document of the 1848 revolutions and of the American engagement with European democracy.

title: Twice-Told Tales
description: Published in 1837 and Hawthorne's first collection: eighteen tales and sketches, mostly of the Puritan past, that established the American short story as a serious form.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Minister's Black Veil', 'The May-Pole of Merry Mount', 'The Grey Champion', 'Wakefield', 'The Great Carbuncle' and 'The Prophetic Pictures', each a study of a single moral emblem in a New England setting.
historical_context: The 1830s, the New England historical revival, the Unitarian and Transcendentalist ferment, and the American gift-book market.
literary_significance: Twice-Told Tales created the American short story and made the Puritan past the central subject of American fiction: 'The Minister's Black Veil' is the founding American tale of secret sin, and the collection established the method that Hawthorne would develop in the novels.

title: The Scarlet Letter
description: Published in 1850 and the founding novel of American literature: the story of Hester Prynne, condemned to wear the letter A for adultery in Puritan Boston, and of the two men who destroy themselves over her secret.
plot_or_argument: Hester Prynne stands on the scaffold with her infant daughter Pearl and refuses to name the father, the Reverend Arthur Dimmesdale; her husband, the physician Roger Chillingworth, arrives to take revenge on the minister, and the novel ends with Dimmesdale's confession on the scaffold and Hester's return to the letter in old age.
principal_characters: Hester Prynne; Pearl; Arthur Dimmesdale; Roger Chillingworth; Governor Bellingham; Mistress Hibbins; John Wilson
historical_context: The 1642-49, Puritan Boston, the Massachusetts Bay Colony, and the 1850 debate on slavery and the woman question.
literary_significance: The Scarlet Letter is the central American novel and the founding text of the American romance: its treatment of adultery, female independence and secret guilt made it the origin of the American novel of conscience, and its heroine is the first fully realised woman in American fiction.

title: The House of the Seven Gables
description: Published in 1851 and the most formally perfect of Hawthorne's novels: the story of an ancient Salem house, a family curse, and the working out of an ancestral crime in the present.
plot_or_argument: Hepzibah Pyncheon, poor and proud, opens a shop in the ancestral house; her brother Clifford returns from thirty years in prison for a murder he did not commit, and the family is haunted by the curse of the wizard Maule and by the greed of the judge who bears the Pyncheon name. The novel ends with the curse lifted and the lovers Phoebe and Holgrave united.
historical_context: The 1850, Salem and its decayed gentility, the American belief in progress and the railroad, and the mesmerism and photography of the 1840s.
literary_significance: The House of the Seven Gables is the great American novel of the ancestral house and of the burden of the past on the present; its combination of Gothic romance and comic realism is unique in American fiction, and its treatment of photography and mesmerism makes it a key text of the nineteenth-century American imagination.

title: The Blithedale Romance
description: Published in 1852 and Hawthorne's most directly contemporary novel: a fictional account of the Brook Farm experiment and of the failure of a utopian community.
plot_or_argument: Miles Coverdale narrates the life of Blithedale, a socialist community, and the fates of the philanthropist Hollingsworth, the beautiful Zenobia and the mysterious Priscilla; the community fails, Zenobia drowns, and Coverdale confesses at the end that he loved her.
historical_context: The 1841-47, the Brook Farm community and American Fourierism, and the women's rights movement and the woman question.
literary_significance: The Blithedale Romance is the central American fictional treatment of the utopian community and one of the first American novels about the position of women: Zenobia is the finest portrait of the woman reformer in American fiction, and the novel's analysis of the failure of the Transcendentalist experiment is the most searching of its time.

title: The Marble Faun
description: Published in 1860 and the last of Hawthorne's completed romances: the story of four artists in Rome and of a murder that brings the knowledge of evil into paradise.
plot_or_argument: Miriam, the mysterious painter, is pursued by a shadowy monk; Donatello, the Italian count who resembles the Faun of Praxiteles, kills the monk for her; the guilt of the pair, and the conversion of Donatello into a moral being through remorse, is the novel's central argument.
historical_context: The 1858-59, the American artists' colony in Rome, the Italian independence movement, and the American expatriate world of the 1850s.
literary_significance: The Marble Faun is the first American novel of the expatriate artist in Europe and the founding text of the American literature of Italy: its meditation on the fall of man, art and experience makes it the most philosophical of Hawthorne's books and a direct influence on Henry James.

title: The Snow-Image and Other Twice-Told Tales
description: Published in 1851 and the final collection of Hawthorne's tales: stories of New England, of the artist and of the supernatural, including 'The Snow-Image', 'Ethan Brand' and 'My Kinsman, Major Molineux'.
plot_or_argument: 'The Snow-Image' tells of two children who bring a snow girl to life and lose her to the fire; 'Ethan Brand' is the story of a man who has committed the unpardonable sin by searching for it in his own heart; 'My Kinsman, Major Molineux' is a young man's arrival in colonial Boston and his shaming of his relative.
historical_context: The 1840s, the American gift-book market, and the New England historical imagination.
literary_significance: The Snow-Image contains some of Hawthorne's greatest tales, including 'Ethan Brand' and 'My Kinsman, Major Molineux', two founding texts of the American short story and of the American literature of the Puritan past.

title: Typee: A Peep at Polynesian Life
description: Published in 1846 and Melville's first book: an account, partly fictional, of four weeks among the Typee of the Marquesas after deserting the whaler Acushnet.
plot_or_argument: Tommo and Toby desert the whaler and flee inland, are taken in by the Typee, and Tommo lives among them, learns their language, observes their customs, and fears their cannibalism until he escapes on a boat.
historical_context: The 1842, the Marquesas, the Pacific whaling trade, and the American and European debate on the noble savage.
literary_significance: Typee is the first great American book of the Pacific and the founding text of the American literature of the South Seas: it made the Polynesian idyll a permanent American literary myth and established the genre of the Pacific travel narrative that would produce Melville's own later work.

title: Moby-Dick; or, The Whale
description: Published in 1851 and the greatest American novel: the voyage of the whaler Pequod under Captain Ahab in pursuit of the white whale that took his leg, and the encyclopaedic and metaphysical work that contains it.
plot_or_argument: Ishmael, the narrator, ships on the Pequod with the harpooneer Queequeg; Ahab nails a doubloon to the mast and declares the hunt for Moby Dick, the crew is drawn into his obsession, the Pequod meets the ships of the world, and the whale destroys the ship at the end, leaving Ishmael to float on Queequeg's coffin.
narrative_structure: First-person narrative by Ishmael, broken by chapters of stage direction, sermon, catalogue, essay and lyric.
principal_characters: Ishmael; Captain Ahab; Queequeg; Starbuck; Stubb; Flask; St. John; Pip; Tashtego; Daggoo; Fedallah; Moby Dick
historical_context: The 1840s-50s, the Nantucket and New Bedford whaling industry, the American exploration of the Pacific, the debate on slavery, and the Romantic philosophy of the absolute.
literary_significance: Moby-Dick is the central work of American literature and one of the greatest novels ever written: its fusion of Shakespearean tragedy, cetological encyclopaedia, democratic epic and metaphysical speculation has made it the foundation of American studies, and its whiteness and its Ahab remain permanent symbols of the modern world.

title: 'Bartleby, the Scrivener: A Story of Wall-Street'
description: Published in Putnam's Monthly in 1853 and the greatest American short story: the account of a Wall Street lawyer's clerk who answers every request with the words 'I would prefer not to'.
plot_or_argument: The narrator, a lawyer, hires Bartleby as a copyist; Bartleby copies perfectly for a while and then refuses, without explanation, to do anything but copy — and finally to do anything at all; he is removed to the Tombs, where he dies of self-starvation against the wall.
historical_context: The 1850s, Wall Street and the new commercial office, the American economy of speculation, and the growth of the bureaucratic city.
literary_significance: 'Bartleby' is one of the most analysed stories in world literature and the founding text of the modern literature of the office: its phrase 'I would prefer not to' has become the central modern statement of passive resistance, and it stands at the origin of Kafka, Beckett and the literature of the absurd.

title: Benito Cereno
description: Published in Putnam's Monthly in 1855 and the most disturbing American story about slavery: the account of an American sea captain who boards a Spanish slave ship and fails to see the truth.
plot_or_argument: Captain Amasa Delano of the Bachelor's Delight finds the San Dominick off the coast of Chile, with its captain Don Benito Cereno and the faithful slave Babo; the truth — that the Africans have seized the ship and are forcing the Spaniards to sail to Africa — is concealed from Delano until Babo's final attack, and the story ends with Cereno's death and Babo's execution.
historical_context: The 1799, the Spanish slave trade, the Haitian revolution, and the American debate on slavery after the Fugitive Slave Law of 1850.
literary_significance: Benito Cereno is the central American literary treatment of slavery and of the failure of American perception: its study of Delano's inability to see the truth of the ship has made it the foundation of the criticism of race in American literature, and it is the greatest novella in American writing.

title: Billy Budd, Sailor (An Inside Narrative)
description: Written in the last years of Melville's life and left unfinished at his death in 1891: the story of a beautiful sailor, a false accusation and a summary execution at sea in 1797.
plot_or_argument: Billy Budd, the Handsome Sailor, is impressed into the Bellipotent, where the master-at-arms Claggart accuses him of mutiny; Billy, unable to speak, strikes Claggart dead, and Captain Vere convenes a drumhead court-martial and hangs him.
historical_context: The 1797, the Spithead and Nore mutinies, the Napoleonic wars, and the American debate on law and justice at the end of the century.
literary_significance: Billy Budd is the last great work of American prose and one of the most debated: its treatment of innocence, law and the inside narrative has made it central to the literature of justice, and its unfinished state has produced a century of textual scholarship.
attribution_notes: Left unfinished at Melville's death in 1891; the text was reconstructed and first published in 1924, and the scholarly editions of 1962 and 2017 differ substantially.

title: The Piazza Tales
description: Published in 1856 and the only collection of Melville's stories in his lifetime: 'The Piazza', 'Bartleby', 'Benito Cereno', 'The Lightning-Rod Man', 'The Encantadas' and 'The Bell-Tower'.
plot_or_argument: The volume moves from the domestic comedy of the piazza to the horror of Bartleby, the slave-ship narrative of Benito Cereno, the sketches of the Galápagos, and the fable of the bell-tower and its automaton, a parable of machinery and pride.
historical_context: The 1853-56, Putnam's Monthly and the American magazine market, the Galápagos voyages, and the American debate on slavery and technology.
literary_significance: The Piazza Tales contains the greatest short fiction of the American nineteenth century: 'Bartleby' and 'Benito Cereno' alone would make it a central book, and the volume as a whole is the foundation of the American short story.

title: Battle-Pieces and Aspects of the War
description: Published in 1866 and the greatest book of American Civil War poetry by a participant: seventy-two poems on the battles, the leaders and the moral meaning of the war.
plot_or_argument: The poems move from 'The Portent' (John Brown) through 'Shiloh', 'The March into Virginia', 'A Utilitarian View of the Monitor's Fight' and 'The Armies of the Wilderness' to the elegy for Lincoln and the prose 'Supplement' on Reconstruction.
historical_context: The 1861-65, the American Civil War, the assassination of Lincoln, and the debate on Reconstruction.
literary_significance: Battle-Pieces is the central American poetic record of the Civil War and the finest body of war poetry written by an American: its refusal of triumphalism and its sympathy for the defeated make it a permanent rebuke to the patriotic verse of the period.

title: Clarel: A Poem and Pilgrimage in the Holy Land
description: Published in 1876 at the author's expense and the longest American poem of the century: the pilgrimage of a young divinity student through Palestine and the debate on faith among his companions.
plot_or_argument: Clarel, mourning the death of his beloved Ruth, travels through the Holy Land with a party of pilgrims — a Jewish scholar, a Muslim, a Greek, an Anglican and an American — and the poem records their arguments on religion, science, history and doubt, ending with a vision of hope.
historical_context: The 1857 journey, the American crisis of faith after Darwin, the religious diversity of the Ottoman empire, and the American reception of the higher criticism.
literary_significance: Clarel is the most ambitious American poem of the nineteenth century and the great American poem of religious doubt: its length, its intellectual range and its honesty make it the missing link between the American Renaissance and the modern religious poetry of Eliot and Stevens.

title: Leaves of Grass
description: Published on 4 July 1855 at the author's expense and the founding book of American poetry: twelve untitled poems in free verse, including the long 'Song of Myself', which announced a new voice and a new subject.
plot_or_argument: 'Song of Myself' moves through the American landscape, the city, the body, sex, death and the cosmos in a first-person chant that identifies the poet with every person; the other poems address the child, the poet, the prostitute, and the reader directly.
literary_form: Poetry collection (revised and expanded through nine editions)
meter_and_prosody: Free verse built on syntactical parallelism, anaphora, catalogues and long breath-lines.
historical_context: The 1855, the American democratic experiment, the antislavery and women's movements, the Transcendentalism of Emerson, and the new American cities and crowds.
literary_significance: Leaves of Grass invented American free verse and made the democratic body and the ordinary person the subject of the long poem: it is the founding work of modern American poetry and one of the most influential books in the language.

title: 'Song of Myself'
description: The central poem of Leaves of Grass: fifty-two sections in which the poet identifies himself with all American life — the child, the runaway slave, the trapper, the prostitute and the reader.
plot_or_argument: The poem begins with 'I celebrate myself, and sing myself', moves through the grass as the flag of the soul, the body and the senses, the catalogue of American occupations and persons, and ends with the poet's death and his continuing presence in the reader's hands.
literary_form: Long poem (section of Leaves of Grass)
historical_context: The 1855, the American democracy of the 1850s, the new cities and the open road, and the Romantic idea of the poet as representative man.
literary_significance: 'Song of Myself' is the central poem of American literature and the greatest American statement of democratic identity: it made the long free-verse poem possible and its first lines are perhaps the most famous in American poetry.

title: Drum-Taps
description: Published in 1865 and the finest body of American war poetry: the poems written from Whitman's experience nursing the wounded in the Washington hospitals.
plot_or_argument: The sequence moves from the recruiting and the march through the battles, the field hospitals and the dead, to the assassination of Lincoln in the 'Lilacs' elegy, and ends with the reconciliation of 'Reconciliation'.
historical_context: The 1861-65, the Civil War, the Washington hospitals, the assassination of Lincoln, and the American debate on the meaning of the war.
literary_significance: Drum-Taps is the central American war poetry and the finest poetic response to the Civil War: its plain record of suffering and its sequence of mourning made it the model for the modern war poem, and the 'Lilacs' elegy is the greatest American elegy.

title: 'When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom'd'
description: Published in Sequel to Drum-Taps in 1865 and the greatest American elegy: a lament for Abraham Lincoln built on the lilac, the western star and the hermit thrush.
plot_or_argument: The poet brings the lilac bloom to the coffin of the president, follows the funeral train across the country, listens to the hermit thrush sing in the swamp, and comes to accept death as part of the cycle of the natural year.
historical_context: The 1865, Lincoln's assassination and funeral train, the end of the Civil War, and the elegiac tradition from Milton and Shelley.
literary_significance: The 'Lilacs' elegy is the central American poem of mourning and one of the great elegies in English: its three symbols and its free-verse structure made the public elegy possible in the modern idiom, and it is the founding text of the American poetry of grief.

title: Democratic Vistas
description: Published in 1871 and Whitman's central prose statement: an argument that American democracy must be completed by a literature and a culture of its own.
plot_or_argument: Whitman analyses the corruption and materialism of post-war America, argues that political democracy is only the beginning and that the nation needs a democratic literature, and calls for the creation of a new race of poets and of a culture in which the individual can grow.
historical_context: The 1871, the corruption of the Grant era, the Gilded Age, and the American debate on culture after the Civil War.
literary_significance: Democratic Vistas is the central American statement of the relation between democracy and literature: it is the founding text of American cultural criticism and remains the most ambitious claim for the necessity of a national literature.
